findings.title: Missing heartbeat timeout detection — Rust sends pings but does not track pong timeout
findings.description: Go frp tracks `lastPong` time and checks it against `HeartbeatTimeout` (default 90s; set to -1 when TCPMux is enabled). If `time.Since(lastPong) > HeartbeatTimeout`, Go warns 'heartbeat timeout' and eventually reconnects. Rust's service.rs only sends pings at `heartbeat_interval` via a `tokio::time::interval` timer (line 968) and logs 'Ping sent' / 'Pong received' but never checks the elapsed time since the last Pong. A dead control connection with a responsive TCP stack (no RST) would go undetected until the next write fails.
findings.fix_suggestion: Add a `last_pong: Instant` field, update it on receiving Pong, and spawn a watchdog task/select branch that triggers reconnect if `last_pong.elapsed() > heartbeat_timeout`. Respect Go's convention of disabling heartbeat timeout when TCPMux is enabled (yamux provides its own keepalive).

findings.title: Missing proxy phase state machine for lifecycle tracking
findings.go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/client/proxy/proxy_wrapper.go lines 38-51 (ProxyPhase* constants), lines 138-164 (SetRunningStatus, Start, Stop), lines 194-239 (checkWorker)
findings.description: Go frp maintains a detailed proxy phase state machine: New → WaitStart → StartErr/Running → CheckFailed → Closed. This controls when proxies are registered with the server, handles retries on start error, and integrates with health checks. Rust's ProxyRuntimeInfo stores only a generic `err: String` and `remote_addr: String` without any phase tracking. Proxies are registered once during login, and failures are stored as error strings with no retry cycle. This means a proxy that fails registration is never retried during the session.
findings.fix_suggestion: Add a ProxyPhase enum to ProxyRuntimeInfo (New, WaitStart, Running, CheckFailed, Closed) and a check_worker-style background task that retries failed proxy registrations. Match Go frp's behavior where `checkWorker` periodically transitions New/CheckFailed proxies back to WaitStart to retry registration.

findings.title: KCP XOR encryption comment in session.rs is misleading — Go frp does not use KCP-level encryption
findings.go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/util/net/kcp.go lines 31, 96 (kcp.ListenWithOptions with nil blockCrypt, NewConn3 with nil blockCrypt)
findings.description: Rust session.rs line 10-11 reads: 'XOR encryption (`kcp_compat::XorBlock`) is NOT yet wired — KcpConfig lacks a crypt field'. This implies a gap in KCP interop, but Go frp's kcp.go passes `nil` for the blockCrypt parameter in both `kcp.ListenWithOptions()` and `kcp.NewConn3()`, meaning NO KCP-level encryption is used. The `kcp-go` library supports BlockCrypt (XOR, AES, Blowfish, etc.) but frp itself never enables it. The comment incorrectly flags a non-existent interop gap.
findings.fix_suggestion: Update the comment in session.rs and/or the CHANGELOG to clarify that Go frp does NOT use KCP block encryption. The `kcp_compat::XorBlock` code is unused dead code unless frp-rs decides to add a proprietary KCP encryption extension (which would break interop with Go frp).

findings.title: Group health check TODO describes a feature that does not exist in Go frp
findings.go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/proxy.go lines 72-106 (HealthCheckConfig with Type: "" | "tcp" | "http"), /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/validation/proxy.go lines 49-54 (validation rejects anything other than "", "tcp", "http")
findings.description: Rust health.rs lines 10-26 contain a TODO: 'group health check (Go frp compat gap) ... When health_check_type == "group"'. However, Go frp's validation logic (validation/proxy.go:49-54) only accepts health check types of "", "tcp", or "http". There is no "group" health check type in Go frp dev. Health checks are per-proxy only; the proxy Group field (proxy.go:53) is used solely for server-side load balancing, not health checking. The TODO describes a feature that would not interoperate with Go frp.
findings.fix_suggestion: Remove the group health check TODO comment or update it to reflect that Go frp does not support group-level health checks. If group-level health checking is desired as a frp-rs extension, document it as such (not as a Go compat gap).

findings.title: Missing config store / CRUD API for runtime proxy/visitor management
findings.go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/client/config_manager.go lines 153-464 (ListStoreProxies, CreateStoreProxy, UpdateStoreProxy, DeleteStoreProxy, etc. — full CRUD on StoreSource proxies and visitors)
findings.description: Go frp dev has a complete `config_manager.go` with `StoreSource` that supports CRUD operations on proxies and visitors (CreateStoreProxy, UpdateStoreProxy, DeleteStoreProxy, ListStoreProxies, etc.), config source aggregation, and hot-reload via the admin API. These are exposed through the admin HTTP API. Rust's reload.rs only implements `do_reload()` which diffs old vs new config from file. There is no store/CRUD mechanism, no config source aggregation, and no persistence layer. The admin API endpoints for proxy CRUD are therefore non-functional.
findings.fix_suggestion: Implement a StoreSource trait with in-memory HashMap storage (matching Go frp's source.StoreSource interface) and wire it through the admin API. The CRUD operations should trigger config reload (via the existing reload channel) after each mutation.

findings.title: Yamux keepalive uses polling fallback instead of native yamux keepalive interval
findings.description: Go frp sets `fmuxCfg.KeepAliveInterval` on the yamux config (hashicorp/yamux fork) to the configured value (default 30s). Rust mux.rs line 119-121 notes: 'NOTE: yamux 0.14.0 does not expose set_keepalive_interval on Config.' Rust implements keepalive via a `tokio::time::sleep(keepalive)` branch in the select! loop that drives the yamux connection (this triggers poll_next_inbound periodically). The behavior is functionally similar (both detect dead peers) but uses a different mechanism. Under sustained load, Rust's approach adds an extra timer wakeup per keepalive interval. Under idle, both approaches are equivalent.
findings.fix_suggestion: Monitor yamux-rs for API additions that expose keepalive_interval natively. Until then, the polling fallback is acceptable but should be documented more clearly as a behavioral divergence.

findings.title: QUIC_GO_DISABLE_ECN and crypto.DefaultSalt env vars not configured in Rust
findings.description: Go frp's init() function sets `crypto.DefaultSalt = "frp"` (used by golib/crypto for AES-128-CFB control encryption key derivation) and disables QUIC ECN by default due to known issues on certain OSes. Rust uses `frp-core::encryption::derive_key()` for the AES key and `quinn` for QUIC (not quic-go). The quinn library may handle ECN differently, but there is no explicit equivalent to Go frp's ECN disabling. Additionally, Go frp disables quic-go's receive buffer warning.
findings.fix_suggestion: Ensure the encryption key derivation (`derive_key`) produces identical results to Go frp's `golib/crypto` with DefaultSalt="frp". The QUIC ECN handling in quinn should be checked — if quinn enables ECN by default, consider disabling it for parity.

findings.title: Go frp's ClientCommonConfig.Complete() defaults missing in Rust config
findings.go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/client.go (Complete() method sets TCPMux defaults, poolCount, etc.) and server.go Complete() lines 182-197
findings.description: Go frp has a `Complete()` method on config structs that fills in defaults (e.g., TCPMux default true, TCPMuxKeepaliveInterval default 30, TCPKeepAlive default 7200, HeartbeatTimeout default 90 or -1 depending on TCPMux). Rust's config.rs uses serde defaults. Some values match serde defaults (tcp_mux defaults to true in Rust), but the conditional logic (HeartbeatTimeout = -1 when TCPMux enabled) is not replicated. Config defaults may diverge subtly between the two implementations.
findings.fix_suggestion: Audit all numeric/boolean config defaults in frp-core/src/config.rs against Go frp v1 Complete() methods. Ensure the conditional logic (especially for HeartbeatTimeout and TCPMux interaction) is replicated in Rust's default path.

findings.title: Rust HTTP health check sends HTTP/1.0 requests; Go frp sends proper HTTP/1.1
findings.go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/client/health/health.go lines 167-184: http.NewRequestWithContext with http.DefaultClient.Do (proper HTTP client, HTTP/1.1 defaults)
findings.description: Go frp's HTTP health check uses `http.NewRequestWithContext()` and `http.DefaultClient.Do()`, which sends proper HTTP/1.1 requests with full header support. Rust's `run_http_check` constructs a raw HTTP/1.0 GET request manually and only checks for '200' or ' 2' in the status line. The raw approach handles most cases but may not handle chunked responses, keep-alive connections, or redirects. The Host header is also derived from addr.split(':')[0] which may strip port info.
findings.fix_suggestion: Consider using an HTTP client crate (like `reqwest`) for HTTP health checks, or enhance the raw parser to handle HTTP/1.1 responses properly (chunked encoding, connection: close, etc.). At minimum, add port to the Host header.

findings.title: Rust WebSocket handler relies on raw manual framing for Go frp compat — diverges from Go frp's use of golang.org/x/net/websocket
findings.go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/util/net/websocket.go (WebsocketListener, BinaryFrame payload type), dial.go (DialHookWebsocket with cfg.PayloadType = websocket.BinaryFrame)
findings.description: Go frp uses `golang.org/x/net/websocket` library which sends encrypted frp data as TEXT frames (violating RFC 6455 §5.6 for non-UTF-8 payloads). Rust implements a custom WsByteStream with two modes: tungstenite (client side, sends Binary frames) and Raw (server/manual mode, handles both text and binary frames). The Raw mode is specifically designed to handle Go frp's non-UTF-8 text frames. Rust's client mode (tungstenite) sends Binary frames, which Go frp's server WsByteStream will accept. The interop should work but the Rust approach is much more complex and fragile.
findings.fix_suggestion: The existing Raw frame handling is correct for interop. However, the code (entire WsByteStream implementation plus accept_websocket/accept_websocket_from_peeked/connect_ws_raw) is nearly 800 lines of manual WebSocket frame parsing. Consider testing against Go frps with various payload patterns (binary, encrypted, compressed) to ensure edge cases are handled.
